extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative standards for producing and judging poetry: temperamental marks of genius, stylistic pitfalls, and how critics should properly assess poetic works. Focuses on what distinguishes works of true genius from manufactured verse and on correct critical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: The three sins of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Young writers are likely beset by one of three characteristic faults: (1) doleful egotism and the recurrence of favourite phrases (trite and licentious), (2) low, creeping language and thoughts under the pretence of simplicity, (3) the indiscriminate use of elaborate and swelling language and imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge illustrates these in three sonnets (reprinted for biographical purposes). Treat these as common anti-patterns of early or immature poetic style to be identified and avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced diction — avoid florid labour or affected simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction should avoid the extremes of laborious, florid phrasing born of diffidence and the opposite extreme of an affected, artificial simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice should conform to 'better judgment' — neither over-embellish (the early 'labourious and florid diction') nor adopt an artificial simplicity; aim for naturalness and appropriateness to subject and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid imagination and combinatory power
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is indicated when 'the ideas are vivid, and there exists an endless power of combining and modifying them' so that feelings and affections blend more easily with ideal creations than with sensory objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry by the vividness and fecundity of its imaginative material and the writer’s ability to recombine and modify ideas into rich, original formations rather than mere imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanity between fanaticism and diseased indolence
rubrics_metrics.description: The healthy imaginative mind stands between superstition/fanaticism on one hand and enthusiasm combined with indifference and a diseased slowness to action on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether imaginative power is balanced and directed — neither deluded by fervour nor paralysed by disengagement — as a mark of creative maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calm temperament and self-possession as markers of true genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the greatest poets (Chaucer, Shakespeare, Spenser, Milton) display calmness, cheerfulness, and even self-possession in matters relating to themselves; extreme irascibility is not a necessary sign of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging an author's character from their work, place weight on the steadiness and dignity of tone and disposition evident in their writings; temperamental petulance is not proof of creative greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensibility oriented beyond personal interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A key sign of true genius is that sensibility is excited more by ideas, the ideal world, and causes beyond personal interest than by private, self-regarding motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works whose emotional force seems derived from engagement with thought, imagination, and larger human concerns rather than from self-absorption or petty personal grievance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early and sustained devotion to the craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'requires an attention so early, so long, or so unintermitting' that serious poetic achievement is typically the outcome of prolonged, concentrated labour begun early in life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take a writer's sustained practice and long-term commitment into account when assessing seriousness and likely depth of poetic accomplishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth vs mechanical manufacture (works of genius vs barrel-organ literature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern literature risks being 'mechanized' — supplying both instrument and tune — so that mechanically produced, epigrammatic pieces can appear superficially similar to genuine works of genius (the egg vs the eggshell analogy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discriminate substance and intellectual depth from facile, manufactured effects: avoid valuing mere verbal cleverness or superficial variety that 'spares the reader the trouble of thinking.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge by characteristic merits/defects, not accidental failures
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a fallacy for critics to decide on the merits of a poet by isolated accidental failures or faulty passages; 'where there is genius, these [defects] always point to his characteristic beauties.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should consider the writer's characteristic qualities and overall patterns rather than selecting and amplifying occasional lapses as representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper form of critical engagement: reasoned, public, and accountable argument
rubrics_metrics.description: If an author opposes pretensions of individuals, he should do so 'in books which could be weighed and answered' rather than in irrecoverable conversation; critics should present full reasons and feelings within publishable, answerable forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage extended, documented, and public argumentation in criticism rather than ephemeral remarks; this produces accountable, rebuttable judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for genuine simplicity over ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'excellent ballad in the humblest style' is preferable to twenty indifferent poems that 'strutted in the highest'; natural, effective simplicity is a virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value simplicity that communicates and moves over ostentatious, strutting high style which lacks substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting reviewers' reprinting of worst passages dictate reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers often select and reprint passages they deem most worthless, thereby wasting more paper and misleading readers; this practice falsely distorts a writer's reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of reputational judgments based on critics' reprinting of isolated bad passages; seek broader context before forming an overall assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics must possess taste and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism without taste or judgment rewards and encourages inferior authorship: 'the eulogies of critics without taste or judgment are the natural reward of authors without feeling or genius.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight should be given to the competence and discernment of the critic when considering critical verdicts; the quality of the criticism matters to its trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial right to protect and defend one’s works proportionately
rubrics_metrics.description: An author who has devoted his life to literary production has legitimate claims to interest and protection of his works; resentment in defense of substantial wrongs is a creditable duty when proportioned to provocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the moral and practical grounds for authors to defend their intellectual products; criticism should not strip authors of a reasonable claim to protection and response.
